title: Unravelling genomic differences in cerebrospinal fluid: patients with lung cancer with combined brain parenchymal and meningeal metastasis versus exclusive meningeal metastasis
author: Liwei Sun; Jinduo Li; Yuan Lv; Lin Li; Xiaomin Liu
text:
Abstract
Objective
This study aimed to compare and analyse the genomic features in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) between patients with both brain parenchymal metastasis (BM) and meningeal metastasis (MM) of lung cancer and patients with MM only.
Methods
34 patients with lung adenocarcinoma were included in this study, including 18 patients in the BM&MM group, 12 in the MM group and 4 in the BM group. The genomic characteristics were compared by circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) detection in CSF and plasma samples.
Results
The positive rate of ctDNA detection in the CSF was significantly higher than that in plasma, and the variation detected in the CSF was more abundant, especially epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutation (p < 0.05). The consistency detected between the CSF and plasma was poor. There was no significant difference in the tumour mutation burden between the BM&MM and MM groups, and no significant differential mutations were found by mutation mapping and pathway enrichment analysis (p > 0.05). In the BM&MM group, there was a significant co-mutation relationship between RB1 and ERBB4, MTOR and ATM, MLH3 and CTNNB1 and TP53 and EGFR; in the MM group, there was a strong co-exclusion of EGFR and KRAS mutations. Chromosomal copy number variation analysis showed significant amplification in the MM group at the p15.33 bands on chromosome 5 and the 7p11.2 bands on chromosome 7. In the comparative analysis of tumour markers and CSF biochemical parameters between the two groups, no significant differences were found.
Conclusion
This study revealed significant differences in CSF genomic characteristics between patients with simultaneous BM and MM of lung cancer and patients with MM only. These differences provide potential biomarkers for the precise treatment of patients with brain metastases and help to distinguish patients with lung cancer brain metastases with different metastatic patterns.
Keywords: Lung adenocarcinoma, Cerebrospinal fluid, Parenchymal metastases, Meningeal metastases, Epidermal growth factor receptor
Introduction
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounting for 85% of all lung cancers [1]. Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the most common histological subtype of NSCLC, accounting for approximately 40%, and is the main subtype of lung cancer-related death [2]. Despite recent advances in treatment, the 5-year survival rate of patients with LUAD remains unsatisfactory, and in-depth exploration of its pathogenesis and metastatic characteristics is essential for the development of novel treatments [3].
Brain metastasis is an important cause of morbidity and mortality in LUAD and has a very poor prognosis. Compared with other tumour types, patients with lung cancer have the highest incidence of brain metastases, with a rate of 20–56%. Brain metastasis mainly includes brain parenchymal metastasis (BM) and meningeal metastasis (MM). Population-based studies have indicated that the median overall survival of patients with BM from lung cancer ranges from 7 to 12 months, whereas patients with MM often experience a shorter survival of 3 to 6 months, reflecting the particularly aggressive nature of leptomeningeal disease [3, 4]. In clinical practice, some patients develop BM or MM alone, but some have both BM and MM. The 5-year survival rate of patients with brain metastases from LUAD is approximately 4.51% [4]. Studies have shown that there are significant molecular differences between brain metastases and primary tumours, and brain metastases are considered to belong to branch evolution. For example, amplification of MYC, YAP1 or MMP13 may be driving events in brain metastasis [5–7]. In addition, the tumour immune microenvironment of LUAD is significantly different in different histological subtypes, and these differences may affect the biological behaviour and treatment response of tumours [8–10]. Patients with brain metastases have poor tissue accessibility, and due to the presence of the blood–brain barrier, the circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) content in the blood is low, which makes it difficult to reflect the real gene mutation spectrum of intracranial lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), as an alternative liquid biopsy regimen, has been confirmed by several studies to better reflect the genetic profile of intracranial lesions [11, 12]. In addition, mutation information reflected in CSF is useful in guiding clinically targeted therapy in patients with brain metastases. However, BM and MM differ in cell types, anatomy, metabolic constraints and immune environment due to different specific microenvironments. At present, only a small number of studies have performed a comparative analysis between BM and MM mutation profiles [13].
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a tyrosine kinase receptor (TKI) that plays a key role in cell proliferation, differentiation, migration and survival. In LUAD, EGFR gene mutation is one of the common driver gene mutations. These mutations are mainly concentrated in exons 18–21, with the most common types of mutations including deletion mutations in exon 19 and L858R point mutations in exon 21 [14, 15]. Epidermal growth factor receptor mutations can lead to sustained activation of the receptor, which in turn activates downstream signalling pathways, such as PI3K-AKT and MAPK, to promote the proliferation and survival of tumour cells. These mutations play a critical role in the development and progression of LUAD and are closely associated with tumour aggressiveness and metastatic ability. Although EGFR-TKIs have achieved significant efficacy in the treatment of EGFR-mutated LUAD, the problem of drug resistance remains a major challenge [16, 17]. Copy number variation (CNV) refers to DNA copy number changes resulting from amplification, deletion or more complex variations of DNA fragments > 1 kb in the genome. Copy number variation can be used as a potential biomarker for cancer for early diagnosis and prognostic evaluation [18]. Future studies should endeavour to uncover mechanisms of resistance and to develop more effective combination treatment strategies to further improve treatment efficacy and survival in patients with LUAD. However, the molecular profiles of CSF in patients with concurrent BM and MM versus those with MM only have not been extensively studied. Several limitations remain in the current research on genomic differences in CSF between patients with different metastatic patterns of lung cancer brain metastasis. First, most studies have focused on either BM or MM, with limited comparative analyses between these two groups. This gap in knowledge hampers the development of precise treatment strategies tailored to different metastatic patterns. Second, the detection of ctDNA in plasma has shown limited sensitivity for intracranial lesions due to the presence of the blood–brain barrier. As a result, plasma samples may not accurately reflect the genetic alterations in brain metastases.
In the current study, we mainly compare the molecular profiles of CSF between patients with concurrent BM and MM and patients with MM only to further expand the characterisation of CSF variants presented by more subdivided different metastatic locations in brain metastases and identify possible biomarkers with different metastatic patterns.
Materials and methods
Basic information
This was a prospective study. Thirty-four patients with pathologically confirmed brain metastases from LUAD were enrolled in this study. All patients received treatment in Tianjin Huanhu hospital in China between October 2021 and January 2024. According to the type of brain metastasis, the patients were divided into two groups: patients with both BM and MM (the BM&MM group, 18 patients) and patients with MM only (the MM group, 12 patients). The other 4 patients had only parenchymal metastasis. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) patients with LUAD confirmed by histopathology or imaging; (2) brain metastasis was confirmed by imaging examination (such as enhanced MRI), and parenchymal metastasis, MM or both were confirmed according to the location and distribution of the lesion; (3) aged ≥ 18 years, and expected survival ≥ 3 months; (4) patients or their legal guardians signed informed consent and agreed to participate in this study and receive relevant tests and follow-up. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) combined with other malignant tumour history (except cured skin basal cell carcinoma, cervical carcinoma in situ or other low-grade tumours without signs of recurrence within 5 years); (2) presence of serious neurological diseases (such as epilepsy or Parkinson’s disease) or other systemic diseases, which may affect the CSF test results or interfere with the study evaluation; (3) previous radiotherapy, surgical treatment or CSF drainage for brain metastases, which may affect CSF samples; (4) the patient refused to participate in the study or was unable to cooperate in completing the relevant tests and follow-up procedures.
Detection of circulating tumour deoxyribonucleic acid
All patients underwent lumbar puncture, and CSF samples were collected. The collection was performed strictly according to aseptic procedures to avoid sample contamination. Approximately 10–15 mL of CSF was collected from each patient and divided into two tubes: one for cytological examination and the other for ctDNA detection. Fresh CSF was centrifuged at 300 × g for 5 min to separate the cells from the supernatant. Peripheral blood samples were also collected from patients at a volume of 10 mL. Blood was collected into tubes containing anticoagulant and centrifuged to separate plasma as a control within 48 h of collection. Blood samples tested for ctDNA were collected using streck tubes. Plasma samples were also stored in a refrigerator at 4 °C and sent to the laboratory on time. A commercial ctDNA extraction kit (QIAGEN, QIAamp Circulating Nucleic Acid Kit) was used according to the kit instructions. First, samples were centrifuged at 3,000 × g for 10 min, and supernatants were collected. Then, the supernatant was transferred to a new centrifuge tube, and the lysate was added, mixed thoroughly and centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 5 min to collect the supernatant. Finally, the supernatant was added to the extraction column provided with the kit, and ctDNA was extracted from the samples after a series of washing and elution steps. High-throughput next-generation sequencing (NGS) technology was used to detect the extracted ctDNA. A highly sensitive capture-based NGS assay with a limit of detection of 1% was used in this study. The CSF samples from all patients were examined cytopathologically to confirm the presence of malignant cells; malignant cells were found in 80% of the CSF cytopathological examinations.
Genomic testing
Next-generation sequencing technology was used to detect the extracted genome. In this study, NGS detection that covered the entire genome was used. The panel is commercial. The selection of genes for analysis was based on several key considerations. First, the study focused on clinically relevant driver genes that are commonly mutated in LUAD and are associated with brain metastasis, such as EGFR, KRAS and TP53. The study also included other genes, such as RB1, ERBB4, MTOR, ATM, MLH3 and CTNNB1, that play crucial roles in cell cycle regulation, signal transduction and DNA repair and may be involved in the molecular mechanisms of brain metastasis. The gene loci contained in the detection panel cover the known hotspot regions of lung cancer driver gene mutations and can comprehensively detect various variant types, such as point mutations, insertion/deletion mutations, CNVs and gene rearrangements of the gene. The pathogenicity and clinical significance of detected variants were assessed in combination with public databases (including ClinVar and COSMIC) and literature data. Genomic DNA libraries were prepared with the commercially available “OncoScreen Plus 520-gene panel” (Burning Rock Biotech, China). The panel spans 1.6 Mb and captures coding exons ± 10 bp of 520 cancer-related genes in LUAD and brain metastasis. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 instrument in 2 × 150 bp paired-end mode. A median unique coverage depth of 5,000× (range 3,000–8,000×) was achieved for CSF-derived ctDNA and 2,000× (range 1,000–4,000×) for plasma-derived ctDNA. Sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome GRCh37/hg19 with BWA-MEM (v0.7.17). PCR duplicates were removed using Picard (v2.18). Base quality recalibration and local realignment were performed with GATK (v4.2). Single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions/deletions (INDELs) were called with VarDict (v1.8) and filtered as follows: (i) depth ≥ 100×, (ii) variant allele frequency (VAF) ≥ 1% in CSF or ≥ 0.5% in plasma, (iii) strand bias ≤ 60%, and (iv) Fisher’s exact test p-value for strand bias > 0.05. Copy-number variations (CNVs) were detected using CNVkit (v0.9.10) with log2 ratio thresholds ≥ 0.58 for gain and ≤–1.0 for loss. Germline variants were excluded by comparison with matched peripheral-blood leukocyte DNA when available, and by filtering against the gnomAD database (allele frequency > 0.1%). Functional annotation was performed with ANNOVAR and ClinVar. Concordance analysis was performed for genetic variants detected in the CSF and plasma samples. The detection rate of the same genetic variants in the CSF and plasma samples was calculated to assess the concordance between the two sample types in the detection of variants. The tumour mutation burden (TMB) was calculated as the number of mutations detected per megabase pair. The TMB levels of patients in the BM&MM group and MM group were compared, and the differences in TMB between the two groups were analysed. Co-mutation analysis of detected gene variants identified gene pairs with significant co-mutation relationships between different genes, revealing the distribution characteristics of CNV and co-mutation relationship in patients with different metastatic patterns and enabling an exploration of its potential biological significance. TMB was calculated as the number of non-synonymous, coding SNVs and INDELs per megabase (Mb) of panel territory after exclusion of known germline polymorphisms and driver hotspot mutations. Synonymous mutations were not counted.
Detection of tumour markers
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) tumour markers in CSF and related biochemical parameters, including GLU, lactate and ProGRP, were detected using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), following the kit instructions as follows: briefly, the sample was first diluted according to the kit requirements, and standard wells, sample wells and blank wells were set on the microtiter plate. In addition to blank wells, 100 µL of horseradish peroxidase-labelled detection antibody was added to each well in the standard and sample wells. The reaction well was sealed with a microplate sealer and incubated in a 37℃ water bath or incubator for 60 min. The liquid was discarded and the well was patted dry with absorbent paper. Each well was filled with washing solution and allowed to stand for 1 min, and the washing solution was shaken off and the well was patted dry on absorbent paper. The plate washing was repeated 5 times. Then, 100 µL of substrate was added to each well and incubated at 37 °C for 15 min in the dark. Subsequently, 50 µL of stop solution was added to each well to terminate the reaction. Within 15 min, the optical density value of each well was measured with a microplate reader at a wavelength of 450 nm. The ELISA kits used to detect the tumour markers were as follows: CEA (Thermo Fisher, EHCEA); Glu (Biomatik, EKU10868); Lactate (Abcam, ab65331); and ProGRP (Nebulabio, NBE-231790).
Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis of the data was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 26.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA) and R software version 4.4.1. Several R packages were applied, including VennDiagram, ggplot2 and ComplexHeatmap plotting. Continuous and categorical variables were compared by the Kruskal–Wallis test and chi-squared test, respectively. All p-values were two-sided, and a p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
Basic information of patients
A total of 34 patients, comprising 20 men and 14 women, were included in this study. The median age of patients was 62 years, with an age range of 43–75 years. In the overall cohort, 17 patients presented with lymph node metastases. According to the type of lesions, patients were divided into the BM&MM group and the MM group, BM group. A total of 18 patients, comprising 10 men and 8 women, were included in the BM&MM group, with a median age of 62 years and an age range of 43–75 years, and 13 patients had lymph node metastasis. A total of 12 patients, comprising 7 men and 5 women, were included in the MM group, with a median age of 62 years and an age range of 55–71 years, and 4 patients had lymph node metastasis (Table 1). There was no significant difference in basic data between the two groups. A total of 4 patients, comprising 3 men and 1 woman, were included in the BM group, with a median age of 60 years and an range of 52-73 years, and 0 patient had lymph node metastsis (Table 1).

Among the 34 patients, the mutation profiles were as follows: 16 patients (47.1%) had EGFR mutations, 8 (23.5%) had KRAS mutations, 4 (11.8%) had TP53 mutations and the remaining 6 (17.6%) had other mutations or were wild-type for the common driver genes. In the BM&MM group, 10 patients (55.6%) had EGFR mutations, 4 (22.2%) had KRAS mutations and 2 (11.1%) had TP53 mutations. In the MM group, 6 patients (50.0%) had EGFR mutations, 4 (33.3%) had KRAS mutations and 2 (16.7%) had TP53 mutations. This breakdown provides context for the genetic heterogeneity within the cohort and highlights the prevalence of specific driver mutations in each group.
Comparative analysis of circulating tumour deoxyribonucleic acid detection in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma samples
In this study, ctDNA testing in CSF and plasma samples from 34 patients with brain metastases from LUAD was performed to assess differences between the two sample types in terms of ctDNA detection rate and variant richness. The results showed that 91.6% of the total variation rate was detected in the CSF samples, whereas only 24.6% of the total variation rate was detected in the plasma samples. In the detection of single nucleotide variants and insertion or deletion variants (INDELs) of the genome, they were found in 78.5% of the CSF samples and in 41.6% of the plasma samples. However, in CNV detection of the genome, they were found in 100% of the CSF samples, whereas they were not detected in the plasma samples (Fig. 1A). Compared with paired samples, the CSF samples were significantly more positive than the plasma samples, and the maximum mutation frequency of the genome was significantly higher in the CSF samples than in the plasma samples (Fig. 1B).
Comparative analysis of sequencing results of cerebrospinal fluid and plasma samples
Subsequently, a comprehensive genomic sequencing analysis was performed of ctDNA in the CSF and plasma samples from 34 patients with brain metastases from LUAD using NGS technology to explore in depth the differences in genetic variant characteristics between the two sample types. The analysis showed that more abundant variants were detected in the CSF, and most of them belonged to private variants. Especially for the important driver mutation EGFR, poor concordance was detected between the two types (Fig. 2). The CSF samples had significantly higher positive rates and variant richness in ctDNA detection than the plasma samples, especially regarding driver gene mutations associated with intracranial lesions with higher sensitivity.
Overall comparative analysis between the combined brain parenchymal and meningeal metastasis group and the meningeal metastasis only group
A comprehensive comparative analysis was performed of CSF genomic characteristics between patients in the BM&MM group and the MM group. The results showed that there was no significant difference in the TMB between the BM&MM and MM groups (p = 0.755) (Fig. 3A), and further mutation mapping analysis showed that the gene mutation profiles of the BM&MM and MM groups were globally similar, and no significantly different mutant genes were found (Fig. 3B–D). In the BM&MM group, a significant co-mutation relationship was found between the RB1 and ERBB4 genes (p < 0.05); furthermore, the MTOR and ATM, MLH3 and CTNNB1 and TP53 and EGFR genes also showed a significant co-mutation phenomenon (p < 0.05) (Fig. 3E). In contrast, there was a strong co-exclusion between EGFR and KRAS gene mutations in the MM group (p < 0.05) (Fig. 3F). The above analysis results indicate potential biological differences in patients with brain metastases from lung cancer under different patterns of metastasis.
Copy number variation mutation characteristics between the combined brain parenchymal and meningeal metastasis group and the meningeal metastasis only group
A CNV analysis was performed of the CSF samples from patients in the BM&MM and MM groups. In the BM&MM group, no significant regions of chromosomal CNV were found. However, in the MM group, a significant amplification was observed in the p15.33 and 7p11.2 bands of chromosome 5 (Fig. 4A–C). Both chromosome 5p15.33 and chromosome 7p11.2 bands contain multiple important genes that play critical roles in embryonic development, cellular function and tissue formation. The significant amplification of the p15.33 bands on chromosome 5 and 7p11.2 bands on chromosome 7 in the MM group suggests that meningeal metastases may have unique biological properties.
Comparison of tumour markers and cerebrospinal fluid biochemical parameters between the combined brain parenchymal and meningeal metastasis group and the meningeal metastasis only group
To further investigate the effect of different metastatic patterns on the levels of tumour markers and biochemical parameters in the CSF of patients, a detailed detection and comparative analysis of CSF samples from the two groups of patients was performed. Carcinoembryonic antigen tumour markers were detected in the CSF, along with biochemical parameters, including GLU, lactate and ProGRP. The analysis results showed that no significant differences were found in the comparative analysis of tumour markers and CSF biochemical parameters between the BM&MM and MM groups (Fig. 5A–D). Nevertheless, these results suggest that single tumour markers or biochemical markers may not provide sufficient information when assessing disease and metastatic patterns in patients with brain metastases from lung cancer. Combined testing is needed to assess the patient’s disease and metastatic pattern more fully.
Discussion
In this study, we compared and analysed the CSF genomic characteristics between patients with lung cancer with both BM and MM and patients with lung cancer with MM only, revealing potential biological differences in patients with brain metastasis of lung cancer under different metastasis patterns. Thirty-four patients with brain metastases from LUAD were enrolled in this study. The positive rate of ctDNA detection in CSF was significantly higher than that in plasma by ctDNA detection in CSF and plasma samples, genomic detection in tumour tissues and pathway enrichment analysis, and the variants detected in CSF were richer, especially in EGFR mutations. In addition, the significant co-mutation relationship between RB1 and ERBB4, MTOR and ATM, MLH3 and CTNNB1 and TP53 and EGFR in the BM&MM group, as well as the co-exclusion phenomenon of EGFR and KRAS mutations and the significant amplification of the p15.33 bands on chromosome 5 and 7p11.2 bands on chromosome 7 in the MM group, suggest unique biological mechanisms that may be involved in different metastatic patterns. In this study, we found no significant difference in the TMB between the BM&MM and MM groups (p = 0.755). This result may be due to multiple factors. Brain parenchymal metastasis and MM differ significantly in cell types, anatomy, metabolic constraints and immune microenvironment, and these differences may result in tumour cells with different patterns of metastasis having different genetic mutation profiles and evolutionary paths. The relatively small sample size included in this study may be another important reason for the failure to detect significant differences in TMB. Smaller sample sizes may result in insufficient statistical power to detect differences in TMB between the two groups accurately. Future studies need to consider these factors and further explore the differences of TMB in different modes of metastasis and its clinical significance by expanding the sample size and adopting more advanced detection techniques.
In this study, the positive rate of ctDNA detection in the CSF samples was as high as 91.6%, whereas that in plasma samples was only 24.6%. Single nucleotide variants and INDELs were detected in 78.5% of the CSF samples, whereas they were detected in only 41.6% of the plasma samples. Chromosomal CNV detection was positive in 100% of the CSF samples, while there was no detection in the plasma samples. Several studies have also shown that CSF samples have higher sensitivity in detecting ctDNA in intracranial lesions [19–21]. Nakano Y et al. [19] reported higher sensitivity of ctDNA detection in the CSF of patients with central nervous system germ cell tumours. In the study by Kim SJ et al. [20], the utility of CSF ctDNA sequencing as a noninvasive diagnostic tool for detecting central nervous system involvement in patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was explored. We hypothesise that direct CSF contact with brain tissue and meninges enables more direct access to ctDNA from intracranial lesions. In contrast, ctDNA in plasma is mainly derived from the systemic circulation and is poorly represented for intracranial lesions. In addition, the presence of the blood–brain barrier restricts ctDNA from the blood to the CSF but also restricts ctDNA from the CSF to the blood. Cerebrospinal fluid samples have greater sensitivity for detecting important driver mutations, such as EGFR. In this study, there was poor concordance in the detection of EGFR mutations between CSF and plasma samples. Because plasma samples have limitations in detecting ctDNA in intracranial lesions, they are of limited value when guiding the treatment of patients with brain metastases. Cerebrospinal fluid samples have higher sensitivity and specificity in detecting ctDNA in intracranial lesions and can more accurately reflect genetic variants in intracranial lesions. They are of great value in guiding clinically targeted therapy in patients with brain metastases and should be the preferred sample type for testing patients with brain metastases, particularly those who require accurate assessment of genetic alterations in intracranial lesions. Cerebrospinal fluid samples can more accurately reflect genetic variants in intracranial lesions and help guide targeted therapy in patients with brain metastases.
In this study, we found a significant difference in gene mutation patterns between patients with lung cancer with both BM and MM and patients with MM only. Specifically, there was a significant co-mutation relationship between the RB1 and ERBB4 genes in the BM&MM group, and there was also a significant co-mutation phenomenon between the MTOR and ATM genes. In contrast, there was a strong co-exclusion between EGFR and KRAS gene mutations in the MM group. The RB1 gene plays a key role in cell cycle regulation, and its mutation may lead to uncontrolled cell cycle and promote tumour cell proliferation [22]. The ERBB4 gene is a member of the EGFR family involved in cell signalling, proliferation and survival [23]. Co-mutations in RB1 and ERBB4 may act synergistically to enhance the proliferative capacity and invasiveness of tumour cells, thereby promoting simultaneous metastasis of lung cancer cells in the brain parenchyma and meninges. This co-mutation relationship may reflect the dual selective pressure on tumour cells by the brain parenchyma and meningeal microenvironment, prompting tumour cells to adapt and grow simultaneously at both sites. The MTOR gene is a key regulator of cell growth and metabolism, and its mutation can lead to abnormal cell metabolism and accelerated proliferation [24]. The ATM gene plays an important role in DNA damage repair, and its mutation may lead to increased cellular tolerance to DNA damage [25]. Co-mutations in MTOR and ATM may promote simultaneous metastasis of lung cancer cells in the brain parenchyma and meninges by affecting cellular metabolism and DNA damage repair mechanisms and enhancing the viability and adaptability of tumour cells. In the MM group, there was a strong co-exclusion between EGFR and KRAS mutations, which may be related to the particularity of the meningeal microenvironment. Mutations in EGFR promote tumour cell proliferation and survival mainly through activation of downstream signalling pathways, such as PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways [26]. Mutations in KRAS then promote cell proliferation and survival by activating the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling pathway [27]. Recent single-cell and spatial-transcriptomic studies have begun to dissect the evolutionary trajectories of brain metastases, demonstrating that leptomeningeal and parenchymal lesions are seeded by distinct sub-clones that acquire site-specific copy-number alterations and transcriptional programs [28]. These data align with our observation that MM-only cases display unique amplifications at 5p15.33 and 7p11.2, whereas BM&MM lesions are enriched for co-mutations in RB1/ERBB4 and MTOR/ATM, suggesting convergent but microenvironment-driven selection pressures. The co-exclusion of EGFR and KRAS mutations may reflect a specific selective pressure on tumour cell signalling pathways in the meningeal microenvironment, making it difficult for tumour cells carrying both mutations to survive and proliferate simultaneously in the meninges. These differences in gene mutation patterns provide potential biomarkers for the precise treatment of brain metastases from lung cancer. Future studies are needed to further validate the biological function and clinical significance of these gene mutation patterns.
In this study, we performed CNV analysis of CSF samples from patients with lung cancer with both BM and MM versus patients with MM only. The results showed that no significant chromosomal CNV regions were found in the BM&MM group, whereas significant amplification of chromosome 5p15.33 and chromosome 7p11.2 bands was observed in the MM group. The chromosome 5p15.33 and chromosome 7p11.2 bands contain multiple important genes that play critical roles in embryonic development, cellular function and tissue formation [29]. The chromosome 7p11.2 band contains the EGFR gene, and its amplification may lead to excessive activation of the EGFR signalling pathway, thereby promoting the proliferation and survival of tumour cells [30]. Activation of the EGFR gene is closely associated with the development and progression of a variety of tumours, especially in tumours such as NSCLC and glioma, one of the NSCLC driver genes [31]. The significant amplification of the p11.2 band on chromosome 7 in the MM group is directly related to the location of the EGFR gene. This amplification may lead to overexpression of the EGFR gene, thereby enhancing its role in MM. Amplification of the EGFR gene has been demonstrated to be associated with tumour aggressiveness and poor prognosis in central nervous system tumours, such as gliomas [32, 33]. In MM of lung cancer, EGFR gene amplification may similarly promote the adaptability and invasiveness of tumour cells in the meningeal microenvironment. Future studies are needed to further validate the biological function of this amplification and explore its potential application in clinical therapy. Further validation of the biological function and clinical significance of these CNV features is also required. The effects of these gene amplifications on the biological behaviour of tumour cells were verified by cell experiments and animal models. In addition, multicentre studies and analyses with larger sample sizes will help to further confirm these findings and explore their generalisability across lung cancer subtypes and patterns of brain metastases.
This study analysed the genomic characteristics of CSF in patients with lung cancer with brain metastases and revealed significant differences between patients with both BM and MM and those with MM only. The detection rate of ctDNA in CSF was significantly higher than that in plasma, especially for EGFR mutations. In the BM&MM group, significant co-mutations were found between genes such as RB1 and ERBB4 and MTOR and ATM. In contrast, a strong mutual exclusion between EGFR and KRAS mutations was observed in the MM group. Additionally, significant chromosomal amplifications at bands 5p15.33 and 7p11.2 were identified in the MM group. Moreover, the field has moved toward integrating ultra-deep CSF ctDNA profiling with methylation and fragmentomic signatures to improve the sensitivity for micrometastatic disease [34, 35]. Our finding that CSF ctDNA detects 91.6% of all variants while plasma detects only 24.6% corroborates these newer benchmarks and underscores the necessity of CSF-based liquid biopsy when imaging lacks the resolution to identify early leptomeningeal spread. These findings not only provide potential biomarkers for the precision treatment of lung cancer brain metastasis but also highlight the unique advantages of CSF as a liquid biopsy sample for detecting intracranial lesions. They help distinguish patients with different metastatic patterns and provide a basis for selecting clinical treatment strategies.
However, some limitations remain in this study. First, the small number of patients included in this study may lead to less reliable results and may affect the generalisability of the conclusions. Future sample size expansion is needed to further validate the findings of this study. Second, while significant co-mutational relationships and CNV differences were identified in this study, no functional validation experiments were performed to determine whether these genetic variants were biologically functional. Further verification of the functional significance of these genetic variants through cellular experiments and animal models is needed. Finally, there are some limitations in the imaging diagnosis of MM. Although imaging studies are currently the mainstay of diagnosis for meningeal metastases, their ability to detect micrometastases is limited. Many patients may have microscopic dissemination that is not visible on imaging, and these micrometastases may have been present early in the disease but have not reached radiographically detectable size or density. Future studies need to combine more advanced imaging techniques to assess the extent of meningeal metastases more fully.
Conclusion
The study revealed potential biological differences in patients with lung cancer with brain metastases with different patterns of metastasis by comparing CSF genomic characteristics between patients with lung cancer with both BM and MM and those with MM only. This finding further confirms the unique advantage of CSF as a liquid biopsy sample in detecting genetic variants in intracranial lesions. In this study, we compared the CSF genomic characteristics of patients with both BM and MM with patients with MM only and found a significant co-mutation relationship between RB1 and ERBB4, MTOR and ATM, MLH3 and CTNNB1 and TP53 and EGFR in the BM&MM group, whereas EGFR and KRAS mutations in the MM group had a strong co-rejection phenomenon. In addition, there were significant amplifications in the chromosome 5p15.33 and chromosome 7p11.2 bands in the MM group; these findings suggest unique biological mechanisms that may be involved in different patterns of metastasis. These results not only enrich the understanding of molecular mechanisms of lung cancer brain metastasis but also provide potential biomarkers for distinguishing lung cancer brain metastasis patients with different metastatic patterns.
